problem.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ be a cubic Bézier curve determined by points $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ .﻿
Let $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ be the $$\text{B-spline}$$ in Exercise 2, with control points $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ .﻿

Let $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ and $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ be cubic Bézier curves with control points $$\{\textbf{p}_{0},\textbf{p}_{1},\textbf{p}_{2},\textbf{p}_{3}\}$$ and $$\left\{ \textbf{p}_{3},\textbf{p}_{4},\textbf{p}_{5},\textbf{p}_{6} \right\}$$ , respectively, so that $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ and $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ are joined at $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ . The following questions refer to the curve consisting of $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ followed by $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ . For simplicity, assume that the curve is in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ .﻿

A $$\text{B-spline}$$ is built out of $$\text{B-spline}$$ segments, described in Exercise 2. Let $$\textbf{p}_{0},\ldots,\textbf{p}_{4}$$ be control points. For $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ , let $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ and $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ be determined by the geometry matrices $$[\begin{matrix} \mathbf{p}_{0} & \mathbf{p}_{1} & \mathbf{p}_{2} & \mathbf{p}_{3} \end{matrix}]$$ and $$[\begin{matrix} \mathbf{p}_{1} & \mathbf{p}_{2} & \mathbf{p}_{3} & \mathbf{p}_{4} \end{matrix}]$$ , respectively. Notice how the two segments share three control points. The two segments do not overlap, however—they join at a common endpoint, close to $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ .﻿

Let $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ and $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ be Bézier curves from Exercise 5, and suppose the combined curve has $$C^{2}$$ continuity (which includes $$C^{1}$$ continuity) at $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ . Set $$\mathbf{x}''(1) = \mathbf{y}''(0)$$ and show that $$\textbf{p}_{5}$$ is completely determined by $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ . Thus, the points $$\textbf{p}_{0},\ldots,\textbf{p}_{3}$$ and the $$C^{2}$$ condition determine all but one of the control points for $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ .﻿

Let $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ and $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ be segments of a $$\text{B-spline}$$ as in Exercise 6. Show that the curve has $$C^{2}$$ continuity (as well as $$C^{1}$$ continuity) at $$\textbf{x}(1)$$ . That is, show that $$\textbf{x}^{ \text{\prime\prime} }(1) = \textbf{y}^{ \text{\prime\prime} }(0)$$ . This higher-order continuity is desirable in CAD applications such as automotive body design, since the curves and surfaces appear much smoother. However, $$\text{B-spline}$$ require three times the computation of Bézier curves, for curves of comparable length. For surfaces, $$\text{B-spline}$$ require nine times the computation of Bézier surfaces. Programmers often choose Bézier surfaces for applications (such as an airplane cockpit simulator) that require real-time rendering.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) The cubic Bézier curve is based on four control points.
(T/F) The essential properties of Bézier curves are preserved under the action of linear transformations, but not translations.

(T/F) Given a quadratic Bézier curve $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ with control points $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , ﻿ $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , the directed line segment $$\textbf{p}_{1} - \textbf{p}_{0}$$ (from $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ to $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ ) is the tangent vector to the curve at $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ .﻿
(T/F) When two Bézier curves $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ and $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ are joined at the point where $$\textbf{x}(1) = \textbf{y}(0)$$ , the combined curve has $$G^{0}$$ continuity at that point.

(T/F) When two quadratic Bézier curves with control points $$\{\textbf{p}_{0},\textbf{p}_{1},\textbf{p}_{2}\}$$ and $$\{\textbf{p}_{2},\textbf{p}_{3},\textbf{p}_{4}\}$$ are joined at $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , the combined Bézier curve will have $$C^{1}$$ continuity at $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ if $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ is the midpoint of the line segment between $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ .﻿
(T/F) The Bézier basis matrix is a matrix whose columns are the control points of the curve.

problem.paragraph: Explain why a cubic Bézier curve is completely determined by $$\textbf{x}(0)$$ , $$\mathbf{x}\prime(0)$$ , $$\textbf{x}(1)$$ , and $$\mathbf{x}\prime(1)$$ .﻿

TrueType® fonts, created by Apple Computer and Adobe Systems, use quadratic Bézier curves, while PostScript® fonts, created by Microsoft, use cubic Bézier curves. The cubic curves provide more flexibility for typeface design, but it is important to Microsoft that every typeface using quadratic curves can be transformed into one that uses cubic curves. Suppose that $$\textbf{w}(t)$$ is a quadratic curve, with control points $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ .﻿

(See Exercise 20.)

problem.paragraph: Use partitioned matrix multiplication to compute the following matrix product, which appears in the alternative formula (5) for a Bézier curve: $$\left[\right. 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 - 3 & 3 & 0 & 0 3 & - 6 & 3 & 0 - 1 & 3 & - 3 & 1 \left]\right. \left[\right. p_{0} p_{1} p_{2} p_{3} \left]\right.$$

From equation (14) with $$t = 0$$ , $$\mathbf{x}(0) \neq \mathbf{p}_{0}$$ because $$\textbf{x} ( 0 ) = \frac{1}{6} [ \textbf{p}_{0} + 4 \textbf{p}_{1} + \textbf{p}_{2} ] = \frac{1}{6} \textbf{p}_{0} + \frac{2}{3} \textbf{p}_{1} + \frac{1}{6} \textbf{p}_{2} .$$

The coefficients are nonnegative and sum to $$1$$ , so $$\textbf{x}(0)$$ is in $$\text{conv\{} \textbf{p}_{0}, \textbf{p}_{1}, \textbf{p}_{2} \text{\}}$$ , and the affine coordinates with respect to $$\text{\{} \textbf{p}_{0}, \textbf{p}_{1}, \textbf{p}_{2} \text{\}}$$ are $$\left( {\frac{1}{6},\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{6}} \right)$$ .﻿

From equation (14) with $$t = 1$$ , $$\mathbf{x}(1) \neq \mathbf{p}_{3}$$ because $$\textbf{x} ( 1 ) = \frac{1}{6} [ \textbf{p}_{1} + 4 \textbf{p}_{2} + \textbf{p}_{3} ] = \frac{1}{6} \textbf{p}_{1} + \frac{2}{3} \textbf{p}_{2} + \frac{1}{6} \textbf{p}_{3} .$$

The coefficients are nonnegative and sum to $$1$$ , so $$\textbf{x}(1)$$ is in $$\text{conv\{} \textbf{p}_{1}, \textbf{p}_{2}, \textbf{p}_{3} \text{\}}$$ , and the affine coordinates with respect to $$\text{\{} \textbf{p}_{1}, \textbf{p}_{2}, \textbf{p}_{3} \text{\}}$$ are $$\left( {\frac{1}{6},\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{6}} \right)$$ .﻿
